title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
hints: think of the problem as 4 possible states you can be in after processing each day: having bought once, having sold once (completed transaction 1), having bought a second time, having sold a second time (completed transaction 2)
track the best possible profit achievable to reach each of those 4 states as of the current day - buy states are negative (money spent), sell states are net profit

at each new price, update all 4 states in this order: buy1 = max(buy1, -price), sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + price), buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - price), sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + price) - each state can either stay the same as yesterday or transition from the state before it

the answer after processing every day is sell2, which naturally accounts for using 0, 1, or 2 transactions since every state starts at a value that makes 'doing nothing further' always at least as good as forcing a trade

initialize buy1 and buy2 to negative infinity (or a very small number) conceptually, since you can't be 'holding a share' before the array starts, but sell1 and sell2 both start at 0 since 'not having traded yet' has 0 profit
commonMistakes: forcing exactly 2 transactions to be used even when the prices only support 1 profitable trade, instead of letting each state naturally cap at the best achievable value
processing the second buy/sell pair using the raw price history independently of the first pair, instead of chaining sell1 into buy2's calculation so the two transactions never overlap in time

updating the 4 states in the wrong order within a single day's pass (e.g. updating buy2 before sell1 has been updated for that same day), which lets a transaction use profit from a sale that supposedly hasn't happened yet
initializing the buy states to 0 instead of negative infinity or -price, which allows a phantom free purchase and inflates the profit

content.problemStatement:
You're given a list of daily stock prices, one price per day, in order. You may complete at most 2 buy-sell transactions total, where a transaction is one buy followed later by one sell. You must sell your current share before you can buy again, and you can never hold more than one share at a time.

**Return the maximum total profit achievable.**

You don't need to use both transactions if using fewer, or none, is more profitable.
constraints: at most 2 transactions are allowed, and you cannot hold more than one share at a time
notes: prices are strictly decreasing (best answer is 0, make no trades)
prices are strictly increasing (a single transaction spanning the whole array is optimal, the second transaction goes unused)
a single day of prices (no transaction is possible, answer is 0)
the best strategy uses only 1 of the 2 allowed transactions because a third dip isn't worth trading around

sampleTestCases.explanation: buy at 0 (day 3) and sell at 3 (day 5) for a profit of 3, then buy at 1 (day 6) and sell at 4 (day 7) for a profit of 3, total 6
only one transaction is useful here: buy at 1, sell at 5, for a profit of 4
prices only fall, so the best choice is to make no transactions at all

optimal.pattern: state machine dynamic programming tracking 4 running values as you scan once: profit after first buy, profit after first sell, profit after second buy, profit after second sell, each updated greedily at every day

bruteForce.approach: try every possible pair of disjoint (non-overlapping) buy-sell intervals across the array, compute the sum of both transactions' profits (allowing the second to be skipped), and take the maximum over all choices
bruteForce.time: O(n^3) or O(n^2) with prefix precomputation of best-single-transaction-so-far
